notes.heading: Metallic bonding and the electron sea
points: Metal atoms give up valence electrons, which become delocalized: not tied to one ion, free to move through the lattice.
The lattice is made of closely packed positive ions (cations) surrounded by a 'sea' of delocalized electrons.
Metallic bond = electrostatic attraction between the cations and the delocalized electrons. Always say 'electrostatic attraction'.
Metals sit at low electronegativity on the bonding continuum; metalloids show both metallic and covalent properties.

notes.heading: Properties explained by the model
points: Electrical conduction: mobile electrons drift toward the positive terminal when a potential difference is applied.
Thermal conduction: vibrating closely packed cations and mobile electrons pass kinetic energy along the lattice.
Malleable and ductile: bonding is non-directional, so layers of cations slide without breaking the attraction to the electrons.
Resistance rises with temperature: cations vibrate more, so electrons collide with them more often.
Delocalized electrons also reflect light, so metals are lustrous.

notes.heading: What sets metallic bond strength
points: Stronger attraction between cations and electrons means a stronger metallic bond and higher melting and boiling points.
Greater cation charge strengthens the bond; larger ionic radius weakens it (longer distance to the electrons).
More delocalized electrons per atom gives a denser sea and stronger attraction, e.g. Al gives 3, Na gives 1.
Down group 1, radius grows, so melting point falls: Li 181 °C, Na 98 °C, K 63 °C.
Across period 3 (Na, Mg, Al), smaller radius, higher charge and more electrons raise melting points.

notes.heading: Delocalized d-electrons in transition elements
points: Transition elements have atoms or ions with an incomplete d sublevel; zinc is excluded as its 3d is full in Zn and Zn2+.
In transition metals the d electrons delocalize as well as the outer-level electrons.
The greater electron density strengthens attraction to the cations, giving higher melting points than group 1 and 2 metals.
More mobile delocalized electrons give good electrical conductivity.

definitions.definition: The electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions (cations) and the delocalized electrons surrounding them.
definitions.trap: Leaving out 'electrostatic attraction' or describing it as ionic or covalent bonding.

definitions.definition: Valence electrons not attached to any individual ion, which move freely throughout the metal lattice.
definitions.trap: Saying the electrons are shared between two atoms, which describes covalent bonding.

definitions.definition: The ability of a solid to be pressed or hammered into different shapes without breaking.
definitions.trap: Mixing it up with ductility, which is stretching into wires.

definitions.definition: The ability of a solid to be stretched into wires.
definitions.trap: Mixing it up with malleability, which is being shaped by pressing or hammering.

definitions.definition: An element whose atoms, or at least one of its ions, have an incomplete d sublevel.
definitions.trap: Calling every d-block element a transition element; zinc is not, as its 3d is full.
